promptText: What is the functional difference between a Kubernetes Pod, a Deployment, and a Service?
options: A Pod is a single running container instance (ephemeral); a Deployment maintains a desired number of healthy Pod replicas over time and handles rolling updates; a Service is a stable network identity that load-balances across the current set of matching Pods
A Pod, Deployment, and Service are three interchangeable names for the same underlying object
A Deployment is a single running instance while a Pod maintains many Deployments
A Service is required only for batch Jobs, never for long-running inference servers
explanation: Pods are ephemeral single instances, Deployments reconcile a desired replica count and manage rollout/replacement, and Services provide a stable virtual IP/DNS name in front of a changing set of Pod IPs so clients never track individual Pods directly.

promptText: Why can't a Pod request 'half a GPU' out of the box the same way it can request half a CPU core?
options: GPUs are exposed through vendor device plugins as opaque, indivisible integer resources — the scheduler has no built-in concept of fractional GPU allocation the way the kernel can time-slice CPU cleanly
Half-GPU requests are technically supported but disabled by default for security reasons
Kubernetes only supports GPUs from a single vendor, which blocks fractional requests
GPUs do not have a resource identifier in Kubernetes at all, so no request is possible
explanation: Kubernetes' original resource model was built for divisible CPU/memory; GPUs, introduced later via the device plugin API, are advertised as whole, indivisible units by default, requiring extra mechanisms (MIG, time-slicing) for fractional sharing.

promptText: What role does the NVIDIA device plugin play in making a GPU schedulable by Kubernetes?
options: It compiles CUDA kernels ahead of time so containers start faster

It runs on each GPU node, discovers the physical GPUs, and advertises them to the kubelet as a schedulable extended resource (e.g. nvidia.com/gpu: 4); without it, the node reports zero allocatable GPUs even if hardware is present
It replaces the Kubernetes scheduler entirely for GPU-requesting pods
It is only needed for training jobs, never for inference-serving pods
explanation: Kubernetes has no native GPU awareness; the device plugin is the extension point that teaches the kubelet (and therefore the scheduler) that a node has usable GPU capacity to allocate.

promptText: Why is the NVIDIA device plugin deployed as a DaemonSet rather than a Deployment?
options: DaemonSets are required for any pod that mounts a persistent volume

A DaemonSet guarantees exactly one copy runs on every matching node automatically as nodes join or leave, which matches the requirement that each GPU node independently report its own hardware — a Deployment's arbitrary N-replica model gives no such per-node guarantee
Deployments cannot run privileged containers, but DaemonSets can
DaemonSets run only once across the entire cluster, never per-node
explanation: Device advertisement is inherently per-node: each node's own kubelet needs its own local device plugin instance, which is precisely the guarantee a DaemonSet provides and a fixed-replica Deployment does not.

promptText: Why do most platform teams adopt the NVIDIA GPU Operator instead of installing GPU support on each node by hand?
options: The GPU Operator is required by Kubernetes' core API and cannot be bypassed

Hand-installing GPU support means separately installing and version-locking the kernel driver, container toolkit, device plugin, Node Feature Discovery, and metrics exporter on every node; the Operator packages and coordinates all of these as controllers, turning per-node manual runbooks into an automated, version-consistent rollout
The GPU Operator eliminates the need for any GPU nodes at all by emulating GPUs in software
The GPU Operator is only used for CPU-only clusters as a compatibility shim
explanation: Manually keeping driver, toolkit, device plugin, and NFD versions in lockstep across many nodes doesn't scale; the GPU Operator automates provisioning and upgrades as a coordinated rollout instead of N separate manual sessions.

promptText: Walk through what happens between `kubectl apply` on a GPU-backed Deployment and the Pod actually serving traffic. What is the key mechanism that prevents traffic from reaching a Pod that is still loading its weights?
options: The Service always waits exactly 60 seconds after Pod creation before routing any traffic

The readiness probe: the scheduler binds the Pod to a GPU node, the kubelet pulls the image and requests a device from the device plugin, the container starts and loads weights, but the Service will not route traffic to that Pod until its configured readiness probe begins succeeding
Traffic is blocked by the liveness probe alone; readiness probes play no role in traffic routing
Kubernetes has no mechanism for this — the Pod receives traffic the instant its container process starts
explanation: After scheduling, image pull, device allocation, and container start, the Pod is running but not yet serving — the readiness probe gates whether the Service includes it as a traffic target, which is critical for GPU pods with long weight-loading warm-up times.

promptText: Why is copy-pasting a generic web-app readiness/liveness probe configuration onto a model-serving Pod dangerous?
options: Generic probes are always more accurate for GPU workloads than custom ones

Default probe timings assume near-instant startup; applied unchanged to a pod loading multi-gigabyte weights, the readiness probe keeps failing during legitimate warm-up and an aggressive liveness probe can kill and restart the pod before it finishes loading, producing an endless crash loop
Generic probes disable GPU access entirely for the container
Liveness and readiness probes are ignored by Kubernetes for any pod requesting a GPU resource
explanation: A model server's warm-up (loading weights into GPU memory) can take tens of seconds to minutes; probe defaults tuned for near-instant web services misinterpret this as failure, causing a crash-restart loop that masks the real (non-)problem of slow startup.

promptText: A Horizontal Pod Autoscaler configured on CPU utilization for a GPU-backed inference Deployment never scales out even when users report high latency. What is the most likely explanation?
options: The HPA is broken and needs to be reinstalled

The inference server is bottlenecked on GPU compute/memory bandwidth, which can be fully saturated while CPU stays low because the CPU is mostly idle waiting on GPU work, so CPU-based scaling never triggers when it is actually needed
Latency complaints are unrelated to autoscaling and should be ignored
GPU-backed Deployments cannot use the Horizontal Pod Autoscaler under any configuration
explanation: CPU utilization does not correlate with GPU saturation for this workload shape; the fix is scaling on a metric that reflects the real bottleneck, such as GPU utilization exposed via a DCGM exporter and Prometheus Adapter, or a leading indicator like queue depth.

promptText: Compare NVIDIA MIG and GPU time-slicing as approaches to sharing one physical GPU across multiple pods.
options: They are functionally identical; the only difference is naming convention

MIG physically partitions the GPU at the hardware level into isolated instances with dedicated compute/memory (strong isolation, but only a handful of fixed partition profiles); time-slicing lets pods share via driver context-switching with no memory isolation (flexible, but one workload can starve or crash another)
Time-slicing provides stronger isolation than MIG because it uses separate physical memory banks
MIG is a software-only feature that works on any GPU generation with no hardware requirement
explanation: MIG gives genuine hardware isolation at the cost of coarse, fixed partition sizes and losing access to full-GPU memory per instance; time-slicing offers finer-grained, flexible sharing but no memory isolation, so one tenant can exhaust shared memory and affect others.

promptText: What is the specific risk of using GPU time-slicing for a production multi-tenant inference cluster?
options: Time-slicing has no risks; it provides the exact same isolation guarantees as MIG

Because time-slicing shares the physical device with no memory isolation, one tenant's pod can allocate enough GPU memory to push another tenant's pod into an out-of-memory condition, even though Kubernetes' resource accounting shows each pod holding its own 'GPU'
Time-slicing physically disables the GPU for all other pods until one pod finishes entirely
Time-slicing can only be used with CPU-only workloads, never GPU workloads
explanation: Kubernetes' scheduler-level resource counting gives a false sense of isolation for time-sliced GPUs; the underlying hardware sharing has no memory boundary, so a compute- or memory-heavy tenant can degrade or crash another tenant sharing the same device.

promptText: How should node pool and scheduling policy be designed so expensive GPU nodes are never wasted on non-AI workloads without manually babysitting placement?
options: Manually inspect and reassign pods to the correct nodes every day

Apply a taint to every GPU node (e.g. workload=gpu-inference:NoSchedule) so nothing is scheduled there by default, and add a matching toleration plus nodeSelector/affinity only to Deployments that genuinely require a GPU — making GPU placement an explicit opt-in the scheduler cannot do by accident
Give every pod in the cluster a GPU request, whether it needs one or not, so scheduling is uniform
Disable the scheduler's bin-packing feature entirely for GPU nodes
explanation: A taint blocks scheduling onto that node unless a pod explicitly tolerates it, and a nodeSelector/affinity rule further targets the correct GPU type — together these make GPU-node placement deliberate rather than something the scheduler could stumble into.

promptText: A platform wants to run a latency-sensitive chat-serving tier and a cost-sensitive nightly batch embedding job on the same cluster's GPU capacity. What architecture addresses the specific failure mode of priority inversion?
options: Run both workloads with identical, default scheduling priority so Kubernetes treats them fairly

Assign the chat-serving Deployment a high PriorityClass (and ideally separate node pools or MIG partitioning) so the scheduler preempts lower-priority batch Jobs under resource pressure, preventing a large batch job from consuming all GPU capacity and starving latency-critical traffic exactly when user demand spikes
Disable the batch job entirely whenever the chat service is under any load at all
Give the batch job a higher priority than chat serving since it runs overnight when traffic is lower
explanation: Without an explicit priority scheme, Kubernetes' default scheduler has no notion that one workload matters more than another; PriorityClass-driven preemption (plus optional hardware partitioning) protects latency-critical serving from being starved by a co-located batch workload.

promptText: The Kubernetes scheduler only tracks GPU extended resources as opaque integer counts. How does a specific physical GPU actually get bound to a specific pod, and why does this split matter?
options: The scheduler itself selects the exact physical device ID at bind time, with no involvement from the kubelet

The scheduler only decrements the node's allocatable GPU count and binds the pod; the actual device selection happens locally when the kubelet calls the device plugin's Allocate gRPC API, which picks specific device IDs and returns the environment variables/device file mounts — this split lets device plugins implement MIG or time-slicing entirely below the scheduler's visibility
Device binding is randomly assigned by the container runtime with no plugin involvement at all
Each GPU is bound at cluster bootstrap time and never reassigned again for the life of the cluster
explanation: Scheduler-level counting and kubelet-level device plugin allocation are deliberately separate layers; this split is precisely what allows sharing schemes like MIG profiles or time-slicing to be implemented inside the device plugin without any change to core Kubernetes scheduling logic.

promptText: A pod is successfully scheduled onto a GPU node and gets a GPU resource allocated, but the application inside logs 'no CUDA-capable device is detected.' What does successful scheduling NOT prove, and where should you look first?
options: Successful scheduling proves the GPU is fully working inside the container, so the bug must be in the application's CUDA code

Successful scheduling only proves the extended-resource count was available — it says nothing about whether the device was actually exposed inside the container; check for a driver/CUDA-toolkit version mismatch, a missing or misconfigured NVIDIA runtime class, and whether the device plugin itself is reporting healthy
This error can only be fixed by replacing the physical GPU hardware
This error means the pod was scheduled onto a non-existent node and should be deleted
explanation: This is the classic split-brain symptom between scheduler-level allocation and kubelet-level device exposure: the pod landing successfully only confirms the resource count matched, not that the NVIDIA Container Toolkit runtime correctly injected the device and matching driver libraries into the container.

promptText: GPU-requesting pods are stuck Pending indefinitely, and the Cluster Autoscaler never provisions a new node from an empty GPU node group to satisfy them. What is the most likely cause?
options: GPU node groups can never scale from zero under any configuration; a warm node must always be kept running

Cluster Autoscaler decides whether to scale up an empty node group by simulating whether a pending pod would fit, but it has no built-in awareness of GPU resources unless the node group is explicitly annotated with the GPU capacity it would provide once scaled up — a missing or incorrect annotation leaves it unable to scale from zero
The pods are Pending because Kubernetes limits the total number of GPU pods per cluster to one
Pending status for GPU pods always self-resolves within five minutes without any configuration change
explanation: Since an empty node group has no running nodes to introspect, Cluster Autoscaler relies on explicit GPU-resource annotations on the node group definition to simulate fit; without that annotation it will never trigger a scale-up from zero, which looks identical to a real capacity shortage but is actually a configuration gap.
